summary: The Centralized Conferencing Manipulation Protocol (CCMP) lets a client create, retrieve, change, and delete the objects describing a centralized conference (XCON). It can control conference state, capabilities, participants, and their roles. It is a stateless, XML-based client-server protocol.

eli5.summary: Think of a remote control for an online meeting. A person uses it to start a meeting, add or remove people, and change settings, and the meeting server obeys.

questions: protocol to create and change conferences
subtitle: A stateless, XML-over-HTTP protocol for creating and changing online conferences, their participants and their roles.

tldr.problem: A centralized conferencing system keeps each conference as an object on a server, but clients need a standard way to create, read, change and delete those objects and the users in them.
tldr.mechanism: CCMP carries XML request and response messages, based on the XCON data model, in the bodies of HTTP POST requests and 200 OK replies. Twelve request/response pairs cover blueprints, conferences, users, sidebars, extensions and server capabilities.
tldr.outcome: A client can build a whole conference through create, retrieve, update and delete operations. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

facts.label: Transport
facts.value: HTTP POST, with HTTP over TLS required

today: RFC 6503 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2012, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It works with the conference data model in RFC 6501, the event package in RFC 6502 and the framework in RFC 5239.

sections.title: Where CCMP Fits
sections.content:
The XCON framework (RFC 5239) describes a signaling-agnostic design for centralized conferencing, built around the conference object: a logical representation of a conference instance, holding its current state and capabilities. The Centralized Conferencing Manipulation Protocol (CCMP) is the conference control protocol that lets authenticated and authorized clients create, manipulate and delete those objects.

Operations include adding and removing participants, changing their roles, and adding and removing media streams and associated endpoints. CCMP follows a client-server model: the conferencing client is the client and the conference server is the server. Requests and responses use HTTP as transport and carry the XML data objects defined in RFC 6501, the conference information data model.
sections.eli5: The online meeting lives on a server. CCMP is the way your app talks to that server to set up and change the meeting.

sections.title: Conference Objects and Users
sections.content:
Conference objects form a cloning tree. Each node inherits attributes from its parent, and the roots are conference templates called blueprints. Nodes can be active conferences or simple descriptions without resources, such as reservations. An object can mark properties as unalterable so they cannot be overridden. Each object is identified within the conferencing system by an XCON-URI, and is described by an XML document whose root element is <conference-info>, following the schema of RFC 6501.

A conference has zero or more users. Users are added one at a time to simplify error reporting, and a cloned conference inherits its parent's users. The server assigns each user a unique XCON-USERID, which points to the user's profile: signaling URI, role such as moderator, participant or observer, display text and joining information. Each CCMP request must carry the requester's XCON-USERID in the <confUserID> parameter, with one exception: a user who has no ID yet and wants to enter a conference.

Registered clients usually have log-in credentials, which go in the subject parameter of a request. CCMP does not maintain subscriptions and provides no way to register accounts; registration is outside its scope.
sections.eli5: A conference starts as a copy of a template, the way you might copy a blank form. Every person gets a name tag from the server, and you show your tag each time you ask for something.

sections.title: How the Protocol Works
sections.content:
CCMP is a client-server, XML-based, stateless protocol, so implementations can handle transactions independently. Its operations fall into four categories: create, retrieve, update and delete. The targets are conference objects (active or registered conferences, blueprints and sidebars) and <user> elements. The lists of conference and blueprint XCON-URIs on the server can only be retrieved.

Each operation is atomic: it succeeds or fails as a whole, and the server MUST finish one client's operation on a conference object before another client's operation on it. The server first checks all the parameters before changing anything. To help clients notice concurrent changes, every conference object has a version number, and every response containing a conference document MUST contain a <version> parameter. A client that was working on version X and gets a 200 response with version X+1 knows it had the latest version; a version of X+2 or more means the object was more up to date than the client's copy.

XML sent to the server must still comply with the data model, even when the client cannot know mandatory values, such as the XCON-URI the server will assign. The client fills such fields with a placeholder of the form AUTO_GENERATE_X, where X is a number unique within the request. The server replaces each placeholder with a generated identifier, using the same identifier for each instance of the same placeholder, and returns the result. A placeholder outside the value part of an attribute or element gets a 400 response, and a domain outside the server's responsibility gets 427.
sections.eli5: Each request is a complete note that stands on its own, and the server finishes one note before starting the next on the same meeting. If you do not know something yet, like the meeting's address, you write a blank such as AUTO_GENERATE_1 and the server fills it in.

sections.title: CCMP Messages
sections.content:
A generic CCMP request has optional parameters subject (username and password), confUserID, confObjID (the target XCON-URI), operation and conference-password, plus one specialized request message. The password MUST be sent when the target conference is password-protected, and the server MUST answer 423 if it is missing. A response always has a confUserID and a response-code, and may have a response-string and version.

There are twelve specialized request and response pairs: blueprints, confs, blueprint, conf, users, user, sidebarsByVal, sidebarsByRef, sidebarByVal, sidebarByRef, extended and options. The plural messages are retrieve-only and return lists, and a table in the RFC shows which operations are valid for each. blueprints and confs accept an optional XPath filter to select a subset.

A new conference can be made by explicit cloning (a confRequest create naming a blueprint or conference in confObjID and no confInfo) or by implicit cloning (no confObjID, with a confInfo describing the conference; without confInfo the system default blueprint is cloned). A successful create returns 200 with the new XCON-URI. A userRequest can add the sender, add another user whose XCON-USERID is known, or let a client without an ID join, in which case the server returns a new XCON-USERID. Sidebars are sub-conferences, either embedded in the main conference (by value) or described externally and referenced by URI (by reference).

Two messages support extension. extendedRequest carries a named extension with its own XML. optionsRequest asks which standard and extension messages the server supports, and can point to schemas for extension elements.
sections.eli5: There is a fixed menu of twelve kinds of request, such as list the templates, make a meeting, add a person or ask what the server can do. Each one gets back a matching reply.

sections.title: Response Codes
sections.content:
Every response carries a response-code chosen from a registry. 200 means success. The 4xx family covers client-side problems: 400 for a malformed request, 401 and 403 for permission problems, 404 when the target conference object does not exist, 409 for conflicts such as modifying an obsolete version of an object, and a series from 420 to 427 for user, password, authentication, parent-object and domain name problems. The 5xx family covers server-side problems, including 510 for a request that took too long and 511 when resources such as user or sub-conference limits are exhausted.

The RFC says that retrying after 400, 401 or 403 is NOT RECOMMENDED, since the request is malformed or lacks permission. After a 510 a client MAY try again after a period specific to the client or server. Any unexpected or unknown code SHOULD be treated like 500.
sections.eli5: The server answers every request with a number. 200 means done, 4xx numbers mean you asked wrongly, and 5xx numbers mean the server had trouble.

sections.title: HTTP Transport and Notifications
sections.content:
CCMP is independent of the underlying protocol, but this RFC defines HTTP as the transport, and conforming implementations MUST support HTTP and HTTP over TLS (RFC 2818). A request is the body of an HTTP POST, and the response is the body of a reply. The media type is application/ccmp+xml, in both Content-Type and Accept, and the XML MUST be UTF-8 with the charset parameter included. CCMP uses a strict subset of HTTP, so a conference server might not be a fully compliant HTTP server. HTTP status codes for CCMP responses and errors MUST be in the 2xx series, and servers SHOULD disable caching of conference information. Clients MUST NOT use the Expect or Range headers, and POST is the only method required.

Many CCMP commands can pend indefinitely, so a client MUST NOT wait forever. It MUST run a timer and close the connection when it expires. Thirty seconds is RECOMMENDED as the default and sixty seconds is a reasonable upper range. A server overloaded with pending requests SHOULD return 510. If a response is lost after a successful request, the version number lets the client catch up.

CCMP is a pull protocol: the client asks. It defines no notification protocol. For clients that use SIP as signaling, the XCON event package of RFC 6502 MUST be used for change notifications. For web-based clients, the RFC mentions an HTTP call back as a possible approach but leaves it to a future specification.
sections.eli5: The messages ride inside ordinary web requests, like putting a letter inside a courier envelope. If the server stays silent too long, the client hangs up instead of waiting forever.

sections.title: Finding a Conference Server
sections.content: If a client is not pre-configured with a conference server, it MUST discover one before sending requests. The result is an http: or https: URI. The RFC RECOMMENDS DNS, using U-NAPTR resolution: it takes a domain name as input and produces a URI. The Application Service tag is XCON, which identifies the conference server for a domain, and the Application Protocol tag is CCMP, which identifies a server that understands CCMP. The RFC's example uses NAPTR records to delegate the service for two zones to outsource.example.com., which resolves to https://confs.example.com/.
sections.eli5: If you do not know the meeting server's address, you look it up in the internet's phone book (DNS), asking for the conference service for that domain.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists attacks such as an endpoint listening to conferences it is not authorized to join, disconnecting or muting others, or creating conferences it should not. It names six concerns: finding the proper server, connecting to the proper server, confidentiality and integrity, authorization, privacy of identity, and denial of service.

Implementations MUST support HTTP over TLS, and the client MUST authenticate the server as in RFC 2818, using the URI obtained during discovery. Because spoofed DNS replies are a primary concern, DNSSEC is RECOMMENDED where needed. The server MUST implement mechanisms to authenticate users, and the subject field can carry a username and password, which is RECOMMENDED over TLS. Once a user is authenticated, the server MUST allocate an XCON-USERID.

For identity privacy, a client can set the <provide-anonymity> element to hidden (others do not know the participant is there), anonymous (others know a participant is present but not who) or semi-private (identity revealed only to participants with higher-level authorization). The system itself always knows who the user is. To limit denial of service, the RFC RECOMMENDS requiring authentication and authorization for every participating client, and the timer in the transport section addresses requests that pend indefinitely.
sections.eli5: Only the right people should be able to change a meeting, and nobody should be tricked into talking to a fake server. So the connection is locked with TLS and people prove who they are. Some people can also choose to hide their name from others.
